title: The verb that waits at the end of the sentence
goal: Build full sentences with verbs, learn the six person endings of the habitual form, and train your ear for a word order that holds the verb back until the very end.
bekal: build sentences in the order **subject — time/place — object — verb**
make a verb negative by inserting *-ma-* right after the stem

dialogs.title: Dialog — Har kuni nima qilasiz?
dialogs.intro: Nilufar and Budi are walking home from the university. Nilufar is curious what Budi's days in Tashkent are like.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Budi, siz har kuni nima qilasiz?
lines.id: Budi, what do you do every day?
lines.literal: Budi, you every day what do-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ertalab universitetga boraman, kechqurun kitob oʻqiyman.
lines.id: In the morning I go to the university, and in the evening I read books.
lines.literal: morning university-to go-I, evening book read-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yotoqxonada yashayman. U yerda uchta indoneziyalik bor.
lines.id: I live in a dormitory. There are three Indonesians there.
lines.literal: dormitory-in live-I. that place-in three-items Indonesia-person there-is.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: Do you speak Uzbek at home?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yoʻq, uyda indonezcha gapiramiz. Lekin bozorda oʻzbekcha gapiraman.
lines.id: No, at home we speak Indonesian. But at the bazaar I speak Uzbek.
lines.literal: no, home-at Indonesia-language speak-we. but bazaar-at Uzbek-language speak-I.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Zoʻr! Men ham inglizcha oʻrganaman, lekin yaxshi bilmayman.
lines.id: Great! I'm learning English too, but I don't know it well.
lines.literal: great! I also English-language learn-I, but well know-not-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Siz juda yaxshi gapirasiz. Har kuni mashq qilasizmi?
lines.id: You speak very well. Do you practice every day?
lines.literal: you very well speak-you. every day practice do-you-?

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Har kuni emas. Dam olish kunlari ishlayman.
lines.id: Not every day. On weekends I work.
lines.literal: every day not. rest taking days-its work-I.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Bir choyxonada. Ustozim u yerda choy quyadi.
lines.id: At a teahouse. My teacher pours tea there.
lines.literal: one teahouse-at. teacher-my that place-at tea pours.

notes: **Look at every line: the verb always comes last.** *Ertalab universitetga boraman* = "morning university-to go-I". Even questions don't move it: *Qayerda yashaysiz?* — the question word is at the front, the verb stays at the end.

**Language names are formed with -cha.** *Oʻzbek* → *oʻzbekcha* (Uzbek), *ingliz* → *inglizcha* (English), *rus* → *ruscha* (Russian), *indonez* → *indonezcha* (Indonesian). The same ending means "in the manner of": *mencha* = "in my opinion".
**Har kuni = every day.** *Har* means "every": *har kuni*, *har hafta* (every week), *har oy* (every month), *har doim* (always). Time words go **toward the front**, before the object.

**Dam olish kunlari = weekends**, literally "rest-taking days". *Dam olmoq* (to rest) is one of the most common compound verbs; the pattern is the same as *ish qilmoq* (to work), *mashq qilmoq* (to practice), *yordam bermoq* (to help).
**Zoʻr! = "Great!"** A casual word used by all ages, like "cool" or "awesome". Its more formal cousins: *ajoyib*, *juda yaxshi*.

grammars.title: Word order: the verb waits at the end
body: This is the biggest new habit you need to build. It's not about memorizing — it's about the order you think in.
after: Read the columns from left to right and you get a correct Uzbek sentence. Translate it into English and the verb jumps to the middle: "I eat bread in the morning." That difference is what your mouth has to practice, not your eyes.
Subject and time/place can swap places for emphasis: *Ertalab men non yeyman* puts the spotlight on "in the morning". What **never** moves is the verb.

The most important part of the sentence stands **right before the verb**. *Men bozorda meva sotib olaman* (focus: fruit); *Men mevani bozorda sotib olaman* (focus: at the bazaar). A subtle tool that becomes very useful after unit 7.

grammars.title: The habitual form: stem + -a/-y + person
body: The first verb form, and the one used most. It covers three things at once: habits, general facts, and firm plans — much like the English simple present ("I go") plus "I'm going to".
after: The rule fits on one line: **stem ends in a consonant → use -a; ends in a vowel → use -y.** Drop *-moq* from the dictionary form and what's left is the stem: *bor-moq* → *bor-*, *oʻqi-moq* → *oʻqi-*, *yasha-moq* → *yasha-*.

**The negative inserts -ma- right after the stem**, and the *a* after it turns into *y*: *bor-**ma**-y-man* = *bormayman* (I don't go). The whole row: *bormayman, bormaysan, bormaydi, bormaymiz, bormaysiz, bormaydilar*.
**Questions attach -mi at the end**: *Borasizmi?* (Are you going?), *Bilmaysizmi?* (Don't you know?). As in unit 1, the stress stays on *-mi*.

⚠️ Three verbs behave a little differently because their stems are very short: *demoq* (to say) → *deyman*, *yemoq* (to eat) → *yeyman*, *qoʻymoq* (to put) → *qoʻyaman*. Learn them as they are; that's all there is.

blocks.text: The dictionary form always ends in *-moq*. To use a verb, drop the *-moq* and attach the person ending.
A habit this course recommends: never learn a verb on its own. Learn *boraman* inside a whole sentence — *Men bozorga boraman* — so the subject-object-verb order sticks along with the word.
They all go before the object, after the subject. None of them moves the verb from the end.
⚠️ *Kecha* means **yesterday**, *kechasi* means **at night**, and *kech* means **late**. Three close words that are easy to mix up; read them out loud in a row until you clearly hear the difference.

*Hech qachon* always pairs with a negative verb: *Men hech qachon bormayman* — literally "I never don't go". Double negatives like this also exist in Russian and Spanish, and in Uzbek they're **required**, not optional.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Uzbek. Remember: the verb goes at the end.
Change into the habitual form for the person given.
Put the words in the right order.
Spaced review — unit 4. Translate into Uzbek without looking back at the unit.
items: The bank is next to the mosque.
There's no table in the room.
